reference.source: Williams Hematology / Nathan and Oski's Hematology of Infancy and Childhood
clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive iron-overload disorder that presents far earlier and more aggressively than classic HFE haemochromatosis, typically in the second or third decade
Caused by biallelic mutations in HJV (hemojuvelin, type 2A) or, less commonly, HAMP (hepcidin, type 2B), both of which cripple hepcidin signalling
Hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism and cardiomyopathy dominate the early picture, whereas hepatic cirrhosis and diabetes tend to appear later than in adult-onset disease
Markedly raised transferrin saturation and ferritin are the biochemical hallmarks, often more extreme than in HFE disease
Cardiac failure and arrhythmia are the leading causes of early death and demand a low threshold for cardiac assessment
Diagnosis rests on transferrin saturation, ferritin, and confirmatory HJV/HAMP genetic testing, with hepatic iron quantification by MRI where needed
Aggressive iron depletion by phlebotomy (with iron chelation when phlebotomy is not tolerated) can reverse or prevent organ damage if started early
reference.pathophysiology: Juvenile haemochromatosis arises from loss-of-function mutations that abolish the hepcidin axis governing systemic iron balance. Hemojuvelin, encoded by HJV, is a co-receptor that amplifies bone morphogenetic protein signalling to drive hepatic hepcidin production; HAMP encodes hepcidin itself. When either is defective, hepcidin is deficient, so ferroportin on enterocytes and macrophages is not degraded, and iron floods unrestrained into the circulation. The resulting non-transferrin-bound iron is deposited in the heart, endocrine organs, and liver, generating oxidative injury. Because the defect strikes the master iron-regulatory hormone directly and completely, overload accumulates much faster than in the partial HFE phenotype, explaining the early and severe cardiac and endocrine disease.
additionalDifferentials: Transfusional (secondary) iron overload from chronic anaemias
Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease with hyperferritinaemia
additionalInvestigations: Fasting transferrin saturation and serum ferritin as first-line iron studies
HJV and HAMP molecular genetic testing to confirm the subtype
Hepatic MRI (R2/T2*) to quantify liver iron non-invasively
Cardiac MRI T2* and echocardiography to assess myocardial iron and function
Endocrine screen including gonadotrophins, sex steroids, and glucose tolerance
Liver function tests and fibrosis assessment, with biopsy reserved for uncertain cases
redFlags: Heart failure, conduction disturbance, or arrhythmia indicating myocardial iron loading
Rapidly rising ferritin with very high transferrin saturation in a young patient
Signs of hypogonadism or new diabetes in adolescence or early adulthood
Evidence of hepatic decompensation or emerging hepatocellular carcinoma
reference.prognosis: Untreated juvenile haemochromatosis carries a poor outlook, with cardiac failure driving early mortality, but timely and sustained iron depletion can prevent or reverse much of the organ damage and greatly improve survival.
pitfalls: Attributing severe iron overload in a young patient to lifestyle or HFE disease and missing HJV/HAMP mutations
Overlooking early cardiomyopathy because liver disease has not yet become prominent
Relying on ferritin alone, which is an acute-phase reactant, without transferrin saturation and genetics
Delaying vigorous phlebotomy while awaiting organ complications rather than pre-empting them
references: Nathan and Oski's Hematology and Oncology of Infancy and Childhood
management: Aggressive therapeutic phlebotomy (venesection) to deplete iron stores is the mainstay of treatment
Iron chelation with deferoxamine, deferasirox or deferiprone where phlebotomy is not tolerated or in severe cardiac iron loading, sometimes combined with venesection
Urgent cardiac assessment and management of iron cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia, the leading cause of early death, with intensified iron removal
Hormone replacement for hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism and management of diabetes mellitus where present
Advise avoidance of iron and vitamin C supplements and excess alcohol, with dietary guidance
Monitor transferrin saturation and ferritin to guide venesection, with hepatic and cardiac MRI T2* surveillance of tissue iron
Genetic counselling and family screening for HJV and HAMP variants
